Presbuteros
pres-BOO-ter-os
n. (Greek)
Greek presbuteros, “elder,” literally older one, comparative of presbus (old man). The same Greek root produces English presbyter and priest (the latter via the medieval contraction of presbyter). In NT usage, the title of the chief ordained office of the local church, used interchangeably with episkopos (bishop, overseer).

Biblical Definition

Presbuteros is the New Testament’s great word for the office of elder—one of two ecclesial offices recognized in the apostolic church (alongside diakonos, deacon). The word literally means older one, the comparative of presbus (old man); but in NT ecclesial usage it has become a technical term for the office, regardless of the literal age of the office-holder (though Paul does specifically charge Timothy, let no man despise thy youth, 1 Tim 4:12, indicating the office-holders were typically though not invariably older men). Several structural features mark the biblical office. First, plurality: the NT pattern is uniformly multiple elders in each local church. Paul and Barnabas ordained them elders in every church (Acts 14:23); Paul calls for the elders of the church at Ephesus (Acts 20:17, the plural); Titus is to ordain elders in every city (Tit 1:5, the plural); James says let him call for the elders of the church (James 5:14, the plural). The single-pastor model that has become widespread in modern Protestantism is not the NT pattern; the NT pattern is a plurality of elders shepherding each local congregation together. Second, interchangeability with episkopos: the two words name the same office. Paul calls the same men in Acts 20 first elders (presbuteroi, v. 17) and then overseers (episkopoi, v. 28); Titus 1:5-7 describes the same men first as elders (v. 5) and then as bishops (v. 7, episkopos). The later development of bishop as a distinct higher office over multiple presbyters is post-apostolic; the NT knows one office named by two interchangeable titles. Third, qualifications: 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 1:6-9 list the qualifications, which are weighted toward character (blameless, husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach, not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre, patient, not a brawler, not covetous, ruling his own house well) and explicitly include the ability to teach sound doctrine and refute gainsayers. Fourth, function: elders rule (1 Tim 5:17), shepherd the flock (1 Pet 5:1-4), watch for souls (Heb 13:17), exhort and convince by sound doctrine (Tit 1:9), feed the flock (Acts 20:28), and exercise spiritual oversight on Christ’s behalf. Some elders particularly labor in word and doctrine (1 Tim 5:17), suggesting a distinction within the eldership between those gifted especially for the teaching ministry and those who, while qualified to teach, exercise their primary ministry in the ruling-and-shepherding function. The recovery of biblical eldership is therefore the recovery of plural, character-qualified, congregationally-shepherding ministry, distinguished from the various ecclesial corruptions: hierarchical bishop-priest-deacon ranking that exalts one elder over others; single-pastor model that leaves one man bearing what the NT assigns to a plurality; democratized congregationalism that erases the office entirely; lax qualification practices that ordain men whose character does not meet the apostolic standard.

Webster 1828 Definition

(Greek term.) Presbuteros: elder; the chief ordained office of the local NT church, used interchangeably with episkopos (bishop, overseer); plural in each congregation; qualified by character; exercising rule, shepherding, teaching, and spiritual oversight under Christ.

expand to see more

ELDER, n. — 1. One who is older. 2. An ancestor. 3. A person advanced in life, and who, on account of his age, experience, and wisdom, is entrusted with the government of the church. 4. In scripture, an officer of the church, also called a bishop or overseer; the chief ordained office of the local congregation.

PRESBUTEROS — (Greek noun, G4245.) Elder; 66 NT uses. Often used interchangeably with episkopos (bishop, G1985, 5 NT uses). The two terms name the same NT office.

Key Scripture

Acts 20:17, 28 — "And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church... Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Titus 1:5-7 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee: If any be blameless... For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God."

1 Timothy 5:17 — "Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine."

1 Peter 5:1-3 — "The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ... Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; Neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock."

Modern Corruption

Presbuteros-shaped eldership is corrupted, in the present church landscape, by the single-pastor model (one man bearing what NT plurality assigns to multiple), the hierarchical episcopal model (raising bishop as a higher office over multiple presbyters, post-apostolically), the lax-qualification practices (ordaining men whose character does not meet the apostolic standard), and the democratized congregationalism that erases the office entirely.

expand to see more

The single-pastor model is the most pervasive contemporary corruption among Protestant churches that retain the office of elder at all. The NT pattern is multiple elders in each local congregation, sharing the rule, the shepherding, the teaching, and the oversight; the post-Reformation Protestant pattern has often collapsed this into the single senior pastor (with assistants, perhaps, but not co-equal elders) carrying the bulk of the ministry alone. The result is exhausted pastors, dependent congregations, and the loss of the mutual accountability the NT plural-eldership pattern preserves. The recovery is the recovery of plural eldership: multiple character-qualified men, ordained to share the ministry of the Word, the shepherding of the flock, and the spiritual oversight of the congregation. The hierarchical episcopal model that distinguishes bishop as a higher office over multiple presbyters is a post-apostolic development (clear by Ignatius of Antioch, ca. 110, but not in the NT itself); the recovery of biblical eldership preserves the equality of elders within the plurality, with such functional distinctions (teaching elder vs. ruling elder, as in some Reformed polities) as the NT itself indicates.

The lax-qualification corruption is the broader and more pastorally damaging contemporary one. The qualifications of 1 Tim 3 and Tit 1 are weighted toward character—blameless, husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach, not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre, patient, not a brawler, not covetous, ruling his own house well, having his children in subjection, not a novice, having a good report of them which are without. Many contemporary ordinations proceed without serious examination of these qualifications; men are ordained whose lives bear credible moral charges, whose families are disordered, whose teaching is at best superficial, whose qualification for the office is functionally limited to a personable temperament and an inclination toward ministry. The recovery is the recovery of the qualifications as a real test, with examining elders and congregations refusing to ordain those who do not meet the apostolic standard, however gifted in other respects. The democratized-congregationalism corruption at the other extreme erases the office entirely, treating the congregation as functionally undifferentiated and recognizing no particular office of elder over it. Both extremes miss the NT pattern: plural, character-qualified, congregationally-shepherding eldership under Christ, with the deacons supplying the diaconal service alongside, and the whole body engaged in the ministry the Spirit has given to every member.

Hebrew Roots

Greek presbuteros (elder, literally older one), the comparative of presbus; the chief ordained office of the NT local church, used interchangeably with episkopos (overseer/bishop); plural in each congregation, qualified by character per 1 Tim 3 and Tit 1, exercising rule, shepherding, teaching, and spiritual oversight under Christ.

expand to see more

Greek presbuteros (G4245) — elder (66 NT uses; the comparative of presbus, old man).

Greek episkopos (G1985) — overseer, bishop (5 NT uses; used interchangeably with presbuteros).

Greek episkopē (G1984) — oversight, the office of bishop (Acts 1:20; 1 Tim 3:1).

Greek poimēn (G4166) — shepherd, pastor (Eph 4:11; the closely related function-name).

Usage

"The elders of the church... the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers—Acts 20:17, 28 uses presbuteros and episkopos interchangeably for the same men."

"The NT pattern is plural eldership in each local congregation; the single-pastor model is a post-Reformation development that loses the apostolic distribution."

"Lax-qualification ordination practices ignore the 1 Tim 3 and Tit 1 character requirements; recovery is the rigorous application of the apostolic qualifications as a real test."
